Exercises for chapter 5 - 6

Hiro, Hendrik, Stefan

19 October 2026

0. Data and train/test split

We use data_ml.RData and keep the 2000-2018 window, as in the Chapters 1-4 homework. The first 80% of months form the training sample and the last 20% form the test sample. We do not shuffle observations, so the test period always comes after the training period.

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(knitr)

load("data_ml.RData")                                   # Load the raw dataset
data_ml <- data_ml %>%
  filter(date > "1999-12-31", date < "2019-01-01") %>%   # Keep only the 2000-2018 window
  arrange(stock_id, date)                                # Sort by stock, then time

features <- colnames(data_ml[3:95])                     # Book's full feature set: 93 predictors

dates <- sort(unique(data_ml$date))                     # All distinct months, in order
split_date <- dates[floor(0.8 * length(dates))]         # Date marking the 80% point in time

training_sample <- data_ml %>% filter(date <= split_date)   # First 80% of months
testing_sample  <- data_ml %>% filter(date >  split_date)   # Last 20% of months, no overlap
y_test <- testing_sample$R1M_Usd

# Small helpers for the text
f4  <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 4)
f6  <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 6)
pct <- function(x) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = 1), "%")
Chronological 80/20 split
Sample From To Observations
Training 2000-01-31 2015-02-28 214821
Test 2015-03-31 2018-12-31 53515

1. OLS benchmark

formula_full <- as.formula(paste("R1M_Usd ~", paste(features, collapse = " + ")))
fit_ols <- lm(formula_full, data = training_sample)        # Plain least squares, no penalty

pred_ols <- predict(fit_ols, newdata = testing_sample)     # Uses training coefficients only

mse_ols <- mean((pred_ols - y_test)^2)                     # Test MSE
hit_ols <- mean(pred_ols * y_test > 0)                     # Hit ratio: share of correct signs

pred_naive <- rep(mean(training_sample$R1M_Usd), length(y_test))  # Always predict the training mean
mse_naive  <- mean((pred_naive - y_test)^2)
OLS benchmark on the test sample
Model Test MSE Hit ratio
OLS (93 features) 0.04580 0.52075
Naive (training mean) 0.04577 0.53206

Answer. OLS has a test MSE of 0.045804 and a hit ratio of 52.1%. Its MSE is slightly worse than the naive forecast that always predicts the training mean (0.045774). OLS is a useful benchmark because ridge, LASSO and elastic net are OLS plus a penalty. OLS is the “penalty = 0” case, so any gain from the penalized models can be credited to the penalty. With 93 correlated features, OLS overfits noise, which is exactly the problem penalization should fix.

2. LASSO coefficient paths

library(glmnet)

y_penalized <- training_sample$R1M_Usd
x_penalized <- training_sample %>% dplyr::select(all_of(features)) %>% as.matrix()
x_test      <- testing_sample  %>% dplyr::select(all_of(features)) %>% as.matrix()

fit_lasso <- glmnet(x_penalized, y_penalized, alpha = 1)   # alpha = 1 means LASSO penalty
lasso_res <- summary(fit_lasso$beta)                       # Non-zero coefficients only
lasso_res$Lambda  <- fit_lasso$lambda[lasso_res$j]         # Lambda for each coefficient
lasso_res$Feature <- features[lasso_res$i] %>% as.factor() # Feature name for each coefficient

# Order in which features become non-zero (largest lambda = survives longest)
entry <- lasso_res %>%
  group_by(Feature) %>%
  summarize(lambda_in = max(Lambda),
            sign = sign(x[which.max(Lambda)])) %>%         # Sign when the feature first appears
  arrange(desc(lambda_in))

top10 <- as.character(entry$Feature[1:10])                 # Readable subset: first 10 to enter
lasso_res %>%
  filter(Feature %in% top10, Lambda > 0.001) %>%           # Hide the collinear region near zero
  ggplot(aes(x = Lambda, y = x, color = Feature)) +
  geom_line() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  ylab("beta") + theme_light() +
  theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 7))

LASSO coefficient paths, first 10 features to enter

First five features to enter the LASSO path (= last to leave)
Feature Lambda at entry Sign
Mkt_Cap_3M_Usd 0.00603 -
Eps 0.00456 -
Pb 0.00456 -
Vol1Y_Usd 0.00456 +
Vol3Y_Usd 0.00456 +

Answer. As lambda increases, the penalty on the total absolute size of the coefficients grows. All coefficients shrink towards zero, and LASSO sets them exactly to zero one by one. At the largest lambda every coefficient is zero and the model predicts the mean. The last three non-zero features are Mkt_Cap_3M_Usd (-), Eps (-) and Pb (-). The negative size sign matches the small-cap effect: smaller firms earned more. The positive volatility sign goes against the low-volatility anomaly, possibly because volatile stocks also tend to be small. A negative Pb sign matches the value effect. These signs are partial effects, measured with the other features in the model, so the readings are conditional.

3. Ridge versus LASSO

fit_ridge <- glmnet(x_penalized, y_penalized, alpha = 0)   # alpha = 0 means ridge penalty
ridge_res <- summary(fit_ridge$beta)
ridge_res$Lambda  <- fit_ridge$lambda[ridge_res$j]
ridge_res$Feature <- features[ridge_res$i] %>% as.factor()
ridge_res %>%
  filter(Feature %in% top10) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Lambda, y = x, color = Feature)) +
  geom_line() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() + ylab("beta") + theme_light() +
  theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 7))

Ridge coefficient paths, same 10 features (log scale) 

lambda_common <- 0.001                                      # One common lambda
nz_lasso <- sum(coef(fit_lasso, s = lambda_common, exact = TRUE,     # Refit at exactly this lambda
                     x = x_penalized, y = y_penalized)[-1] != 0)  # [-1] drops the intercept
nz_ridge <- sum(coef(fit_ridge, s = lambda_common, exact = TRUE,
                     x = x_penalized, y = y_penalized)[-1] != 0)
Number of non-zero coefficients at a common lambda
Model Lambda Non-zero coefficients
LASSO 0.001 18
Ridge 0.001 93

Answer. Ridge paths shrink smoothly and approach zero only as lambda goes to infinity. LASSO paths hit zero at finite lambda and stay there. At lambda = 0.001, LASSO keeps 18 features while ridge keeps all 93. The reason is the shape of the penalty. LASSO penalizes absolute values, which makes setting a small coefficient to zero worthwhile. Ridge penalizes squared values, which barely charges for small coefficients, so it shrinks them but never removes them. Ridge also spreads weight across correlated features (for example the three market-cap variables), while LASSO tends to pick one.

4. Elastic-net sensitivity

alpha_seq  <- (0:10) / 10                                   # 0 = ridge, 1 = LASSO
lambda_seq <- 0.1^(0:5)                                     # 1 down to 0.00001

enet_res <- lapply(alpha_seq, function(a){
  fit_enet <- glmnet(x_penalized, y_penalized, alpha = a, lambda = lambda_seq)
  pred <- predict(fit_enet, x_test)                         # One column per lambda
  data.frame(alpha = a,
             lambda = fit_enet$lambda,
             rmse = sqrt(colMeans((pred - y_test)^2)),      # Test RMSE per lambda
             nb_features = fit_enet$df)                     # Non-zero coefficients
}) %>% bind_rows()

rmse_naive <- sqrt(mse_naive)
enet_res %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(alpha), y = factor(lambda), fill = rmse)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.5f", rmse)), size = 2) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#0570EA", high = "white") +
  labs(x = "alpha", y = "lambda", fill = "Test RMSE") +
  theme_light()

Test RMSE across the elastic-net grid (darker = lower)

Five best (alpha, lambda) combinations
alpha lambda rmse nb_features
0.0 1.000 0.213875 93
0.2 0.010 0.213876 10
0.1 0.010 0.213884 21
1.0 0.001 0.213887 18
0.3 0.010 0.213888 8 
best_grid <- enet_res %>% slice_min(rmse, n = 1)          # Best (alpha, lambda) pair

Answer. The best combination is alpha = 0, lambda = 1, with a test RMSE of 0.213875 against 0.213948 for the naive forecast. Weak penalties (lambda ≤ 0.0001) do worst because they are close to OLS. For alpha > 0, lambda ≥ 0.1 removes every feature, so the model returns the mean. The differences are small: the whole grid spans about 0.000131 in RMSE. That is under 0.1% of the RMSE itself, so the differences are economically negligible. We did not run a formal significance test. Given how small the gains are, we would not expect them to be statistically significant. Since the test sample also chose the winner, the true gain is likely even smaller.

5. Out-of-sample comparison of linear models

best_ridge <- enet_res %>% filter(alpha == 0) %>% slice_min(rmse, n = 1)
best_lasso <- enet_res %>% filter(alpha == 1) %>% slice_min(rmse, n = 1)
best_enet  <- enet_res %>% filter(alpha > 0, alpha < 1) %>% slice_min(rmse, n = 1)

fit_pred <- function(a, l){
  fit <- glmnet(x_penalized, y_penalized, alpha = a, lambda = l)   # Train on training sample
  list(pred = as.numeric(predict(fit, x_test)), nz = fit$df)       # Test predictions, non-zero count
}
ridge <- fit_pred(best_ridge$alpha, best_ridge$lambda)
lasso <- fit_pred(best_lasso$alpha, best_lasso$lambda)
enet  <- fit_pred(best_enet$alpha,  best_enet$lambda)

mse <- function(p) mean((p - y_test)^2)
hit <- function(p) mean(p * y_test > 0)

comparison <- tibble(
  Model  = c("OLS", "Ridge", "LASSO", "Elastic net", "Naive (mean)"),
  alpha  = c(NA, best_ridge$alpha, best_lasso$alpha, best_enet$alpha, NA),
  lambda = c(NA, best_ridge$lambda, best_lasso$lambda, best_enet$lambda, NA),
  `Test MSE`  = c(mse(pred_ols), mse(ridge$pred), mse(lasso$pred), mse(enet$pred), mse(pred_naive)),
  `Hit ratio` = c(hit(pred_ols), hit(ridge$pred), hit(lasso$pred), hit(enet$pred), hit(pred_naive)),
  Features    = c(length(features), ridge$nz, lasso$nz, enet$nz, 0))
Test-sample comparison of linear models
Model alpha lambda Test MSE Hit ratio Features
OLS NA NA 0.045804 0.520751 93
Ridge 0.0 1.000 0.045742 0.531963 93
LASSO 1.0 0.001 0.045747 0.526507 18
Elastic net 0.2 0.010 0.045743 0.531982 10
Naive (mean) NA NA 0.045774 0.532056 0

Answer. Predictive performance: the three penalized models beat OLS, but only in the fifth decimal of MSE, and the gains over the naive forecast are negligible (Exercise 4). Their hit ratios are close to 53.2%, the share of positive returns in the test period. So they mostly reproduce “always predict up”. Interpretability: ridge keeps all 93 features with tiny weights, LASSO keeps 18, and the elastic net keeps 10. We retain the elastic net (alpha = 0.2, lambda = 0.01). It matches the best accuracy with few features, and its ridge part makes the selection more stable among correlated features than pure LASSO. The choice rests on simplicity, not on forecasting power.

6. A simple regression tree

library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)

formula <- as.formula(paste("R1M_Usd ~", paste(features, collapse = " + ")))
fit_tree <- rpart(formula, data = data_ml,                  # Book settings (Chapter 6)
                  minbucket = 3500, minsplit = 8000,        # Large leaves only
                  cp = 0.0001, maxdepth = 3)                # At most 3 levels of splits
rpart.plot(fit_tree)

Regression tree for R1M_Usd (depth 3)

Answer.

  • First split. The tree first separates the cheapest stocks, those with a very low price-to-book ratio (Pb in roughly its lowest 2.5%). This group earns about 6% a month on average, far above the rest. It is a strong value effect, partly driven by distressed stocks.
  • Path to a high-return leaf. Take the other branch (not the cheapest), then small market cap (Mkt_Cap_3M_Usd low), then high long-term volatility (Vol3Y_Usd high). Small, volatile stocks earn about 4% a month.
  • Leaf numbers. The top number is the leaf’s prediction: the average R1M_Usd of the training stocks in that leaf. The percentage below is the share of all observations that fall in the leaf.

All features are scaled to 0-1 by rank, so a threshold reads as a percentile. This tree is fitted on the full 2000-2018 sample, as in the book, so it describes the data and is not an out-of-sample forecast.

7. Tree complexity and pruning

fit_deep  <- rpart(formula, data = training_sample,
                   minbucket = 3500, minsplit = 8000, cp = 0.001, maxdepth = 3)
fit_small <- rpart(formula, data = training_sample,
                   minbucket = 3500, minsplit = 8000, cp = 0.01,  maxdepth = 3)

tree_stats <- function(fit){
  c(Leaves      = sum(fit$frame$var == "<leaf>"),
    `Train MSE` = mean((predict(fit, training_sample) - training_sample$R1M_Usd)^2),
    `Test MSE`  = mean((predict(fit, testing_sample)  - y_test)^2))
}
cp_table <- rbind(`cp = 0.001` = tree_stats(fit_deep),
                  `cp = 0.01`  = tree_stats(fit_small),
                  `Naive (mean)` = c(1, var(training_sample$R1M_Usd), mse_naive))
rpart.plot(fit_deep)

Tree with cp = 0.001 

rpart.plot(fit_small)   # If no split is kept, rpart.plot reports that the tree is just a root

Tree with cp = 0.01

Tree size, training MSE and test MSE
Leaves Train MSE Test MSE
cp = 0.001 3 0.027391 0.045749
cp = 0.01 1 0.027481 0.045774
Naive (mean) 1 0.027481 0.045774

Answer. cp is the minimum relative gain a split must bring. With cp = 0.01 no split qualifies, so the tree is just the root and predicts the training mean. With cp = 0.001 the tree has 3 leaves: it fits the training data a little better and its test MSE is 0.045749 against 0.045774. The gap is tiny, so neither tree generalizes clearly better. The leaf-size limits (3,500 stocks) already act as strong pruning and stop the deep tree from chasing outliers. Without them, a low cp grows many small leaves that fit noise, and test error rises (overfitting). Raising cp, or cutting a large tree back with prune(), removes splits that do not repeat out of sample.

8. Regression tree versus classification tree

add_label <- function(df){
  df %>%
    group_by(date) %>%                                       # Compare stocks within each month
    mutate(R1M_Usd_C = as.factor(R1M_Usd > median(R1M_Usd))) %>%  # Above-median = TRUE
    ungroup()
}
training_sample <- add_label(training_sample)                # Each month is wholly in one sample
testing_sample  <- add_label(testing_sample)

formula_C <- as.formula(paste("R1M_Usd_C ~", paste(features, collapse = " + ")))
fit_tree_C <- rpart(formula_C, data = training_sample, method = "class",
                    minbucket = 3500, minsplit = 8000, cp = 0.001, maxdepth = 3)

pred_C   <- predict(fit_tree_C, testing_sample, type = "class")
conf_mat <- table(Predicted = pred_C, Actual = testing_sample$R1M_Usd_C)
acc_C    <- mean(pred_C == testing_sample$R1M_Usd_C)        # Accuracy = hit ratio for classes

pred_reg <- predict(fit_deep, testing_sample)               # Regression tree from Exercise 7
hit_reg  <- mean(pred_reg * y_test > 0)                     # Correct sign?

share_pos  <- mean(y_test > 0)
share_true <- mean(testing_sample$R1M_Usd_C == "TRUE")
rpart.plot(fit_tree_C)

Classification tree for R1M_Usd_C

Confusion matrix, classification tree (test sample)
FALSE TRUE
FALSE 8875 9113
TRUE 18073 17454
Hit ratios against their own baselines
Model Target Hit ratio Baseline Share predicted up
Classification tree Above median? 0.492 0.504 0.664
Regression tree Positive return? 0.532 0.532 1.000

Answer. The classification tree reaches an accuracy of 49.2%, close to a coin flip, since half of the stocks beat the median each month by construction. The regression tree’s sign-based hit ratio is 53.2%. That looks better, but it predicts “up” for 100.0% of stocks, so it simply matches the share of positive returns (53.2%). Neither tree beats its own baseline. A regression tree predicts a number: the average return of the training stocks in a leaf, chosen to minimize squared errors, so outliers can pull it. A classification tree predicts a class: the majority label in a leaf, chosen to make leaves pure (Gini index). Every stock counts once, so outliers matter less, but it gives only a direction, not a size.

9. Trees across market regimes

fit_2008 <- rpart(formula, data = data_ml %>% filter(year(date) == 2008),   # Crisis year
                  cp = 0.001, maxdepth = 2)
fit_2009 <- rpart(formula, data = data_ml %>% filter(year(date) == 2009),   # Rebound year
                  cp = 0.001, maxdepth = 2)
rpart.plot(fit_2008)

Shallow tree for 2008 

rpart.plot(fit_2009)

Shallow tree for 2009

First split and most important features by year
Year Average monthly return First split Top 3 features (importance)
2008 -0.0269 Ev Mom_11M_Usd, Ev, Mkt_Cap_12M_Usd
2009 0.0419 Vol1Y_Usd Vol1Y_Usd, Mom_11M_Usd, Vol3Y_Usd

Answer. The first splits differ completely. In 2008 (average monthly return -2.7%), the tree splits on firm size (Ev): smaller firms lost less. Among larger firms, heavily traded stocks (Share_Turn_12M) lost most, consistent with investors selling the most liquid stocks first. In 2009 (4.2% a month), the tree splits on volatility (Vol1Y_Usd): the riskiest stocks earned the most. Momentum then works in reverse: last year’s biggest losers rebounded hardest. This is the “momentum crash” of Daniel & Moskowitz (2016). The same characteristic can change sign across regimes, which helps explain why trees fitted on the full sample find little stable signal. These readings are interpretations, not formal tests, and the smallest leaves contain few stocks, so their values are noisy.
